tagline.text: Holy Week fills Marinduque with masked Roman soldiers

children.text: The Moriones Festival runs from Holy Monday to Easter Sunday, when people in Roman soldier masks roam the streets all over Marinduque and re-enact the legend of the centurion Longinus. It takes place in several towns, including Boac, Mogpog and Gasan, and its climax is the pugutan, where Longinus is caught and beheaded.

The Moriones Festival is a religious observance held every Holy Week on Marinduque Island in the Philippines. Participants wear helmets, masks and colorful tunics modeled on the Roman soldiers and Syrian mercenaries of the Bible, and walk through town. The name is usually explained as coming from the morion, a helmet worn by European soldiers in the 16th and 17th centuries, though another theory traces it to the Spanish word for Moors, "moros." Locals also call it "Moryonan," and the name "Moriones" spread during tourism promotion.

At the heart of the story is Longinus, a Roman centurion who was blind in one eye. According to legend, he pierced the side of the crucified Jesus with a spear, and when the blood touched his eye, his sight was restored. When he later converted to Christianity, his fellow soldiers hunted him down, and he was finally caught and beheaded. The festival stages this chase and execution as street theater, with the whole town as the stage. Many participants are farmers and fishermen who wear the mask each year as a vow or in thanksgiving.

Accounts of the origin differ slightly, but it is commonly said that Fr. Dionisio Santiago, the parish priest of Mogpog, first staged it as a play in the early 1800s. Wikipedia gives 1887 and some news reports give 1807, so it is safest not to commit to an exact year. It is also often compared to the Moors and Christians festival of Valencia, Spain.

For visitors, the festival is both a spectacle and a solemn act of faith. Within a single week you will see playful scenes of masked soldiers startling children alongside the Good Friday reenactment of the Way of the Cross. When taking photos, remember that the person behind the mask may be keeping a religious vow, and be respectful. During festival week, small rituals you stumble on in the street are often the most memorable. Rather than chasing only the big events on the schedule, try greeting people resting in their masks in front of a church or in a market alley. A mask is hot and narrows the view, so the best moment to ask for a photo is when someone has briefly taken it off.

From Holy Monday to Easter Sunday, masked soldiers wander through town streets, markets and alleys. They may pop out in front of onlookers to startle them or perform funny gestures, so keep your camera ready.

The climax of the festival is the scene in which the captured Longinus is beheaded. In Boac, sources give different times, such as Easter Sunday morning or Black Saturday evening, so be sure to check the official local schedule.
According to the 2026 schedule, Boac held a parade with Morion groups at 4:00 p.m. on Holy Monday and Holy Tuesday. The schedule can change each year, so check again as the date approaches.

blocks.title: Good Friday Way of the Cross (Via Crucis)

children.text: This procession reenacts Christ's path to Calvary. In 2026, a Kalbaryuhan was reported in Boac at 9:00 a.m. and a reenactment of the Passion in Mogpog at noon. Some participants whip their backs as penance or carry wooden crosses.

The pabasa is a tradition of reciting the Passion of Christ in verse, and around 3:00 p.m. on Good Friday the Santo Sepulcro ritual takes place, in which elderly women exchange Bible verses beside the dead Christ.
Masks are made by local craftsmen from wood, cloth and paint, and are sometimes repainted each year. Many have wide eyes and mustaches, and their strong colors make them popular photo subjects.

blocks.title: A different feel in each town

children.text: Boac, Gasan, Mogpog, Santa Cruz, Buenavista and other towns hold events in the same week. Rather than staying in one town all day, consider the travel distances and visit two or three, and you will see the same story unfold differently in each.

items.title: 2 nights 3 days Holy Week course
items.subtitle: Watching the parade and Way of the Cross from a Boac base

children.text: Take an early bus from Manila to Dalahican port in Lucena, then board a RORO ferry to Balanacan port in Marinduque. Allow half a day including waiting at the port and boarding.
Check in at your Boac lodging and watch the masked soldiers wandering the town center. If it is Monday or Tuesday, confirm the parade time around 4:00 p.m. at city hall or a tourist information desk.
If it is Good Friday, claim a spot along the road early in the morning for the Boac Way of the Cross procession. The procession is solemn, so watch quietly from a distance.
Move to Mogpog to see the Passion reenactment at noon, and check the pabasa recitation and Santo Sepulcro ritual around the church.
Head to the pugutan venue on Easter Sunday or according to the local schedule. The crowds are large, so arrive at least two hours early to get a view from the front.
Return to the port when the event ends. Boats fill up right after the festival, so confirm your ticket in advance or consider leaving a day later.
The exact Holy Week dates change every year. Easter 2027 falls on March 28, so Holy Week runs from March 22 to March 28.

items.title: One-day Good Friday course
items.subtitle: Taking in the Way of the Cross and Santo Sepulcro calmly

children.text: Eat breakfast at your lodging and pack water and a hat. Roads along the procession route in central Boac close early, so check local notices and set out early.
Find a spot near the starting point of the Boac Way of the Cross (Kalbaryuhan). The 2026 schedule listed 9:00 a.m., but it may change each year.
When the procession ends, have lunch at a local restaurant and rest. On Good Friday some places may be closed or offer limited menus.
If you are heading to Mogpog, leave in time for the Passion reenactment. In 2026 it was announced for noon.
Quietly watch the Santo Sepulcro ritual in and around the church. Decide whether to take photos by reading the mood of the people around you.
Wrap up the day and double-check the pugutan venue and time for the next day with your lodging staff or the tourism office.
Good Friday schedules differ from town to town and change every year, so the times above are for reference only.

The festival has no fixed date and changes every year with Easter. It usually falls between late March and mid-April and lasts about a week, from Holy Monday to Easter Sunday. Check the date of Easter first when planning your visit.

The festival falls between the end of the dry season and the hot season, so daytime temperatures are high. You will be on your feet for long processions, so bring a hat and water, and because this is peak season, secure lodging and ferry tickets at least a month ahead.

Weather varies from year to year, so check the PAGASA forecast a week before departure and pack a small raincoat or umbrella for sudden showers. On days when processions stretch through the daytime, leave generous time for travel and rest so you do not tire out before the end.

Boac town center is the most convenient place to stay. Gasan has Club Marinduque Resort, the Tungib coast in Lipata is known for Bellarocca Island Resort, and Boac has The Boac Hotel. Operating conditions can change, so check recent reviews before booking. During Holy Week rooms fill up early and prices rise, so book one or two months ahead if possible.

Eat at local restaurants and market stalls. Marinduque is known for local specialty snacks such as arrowroot cookies, and during the festival some shops may close in the fasting mood of Good Friday, so secure food in advance.

Marinduque is far from Manila, so it is hard to see every town in a single Holy Week. The most realistic approach is to base yourself in Boac and travel to Mogpog and Gasan by vehicle, while Santa Cruz and Buenavista are far enough that each needs a separate day. Many restaurants and shops open early and close in the afternoon on event days, so it is safest to have dinner early near your lodging.
Check the exact parade and pugutan times with the Marinduque provincial tourism office or each town hall. Blogs give different times, which can be confusing.
The Good Friday procession is a religious event, so do not get too close and do not use a flash.
When photographing someone in a mask, ask for consent first with eye contact or a nod. Asking for a tip in return for a photo is rare.
There is little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water. Daytime temperatures are high.
Arrive early at Balanacan for the return ticket cut-off. Check port and operator notices about any special Holy Week registration or extra sailings.
Bring plenty of cash. There may be few ATMs in rural towns.
Dress modestly. You may be turned away from a church if your clothing is too revealing.
A day trip from Manila is practically impossible. We recommend at least one night.
Good Friday events include acts of penance such as whipping and crucifixion, which can be uncomfortable to watch, and some scenes are not suitable for young children.
Schedules and times change every year and differ between sources. Always check the latest official announcements.
Crowds are large, so watch for pickpockets and keep valuables in front of your body.
Masked soldiers may approach playfully, so explain this in advance to children and anyone who is easily frightened.
Some shops and transport stop running during Holy Week, so prepare cash and food in advance.
Sailings may be canceled depending on weather and wave conditions.
The whole island hosts the festival. You can also explore other sights such as beaches, waterfalls and caves.
The provincial capital with its cathedral is one of the central stages of the festival. It is pleasant to explore on foot.
A town traditionally said to be the birthplace of the festival, with a reenactment of the Passion at noon on Good Friday. It is also close to Balanacan port.
A town with an airport and a cluster of coastal resorts. It is reached by car from Boac and also holds Moriones events.
